Not wrong. But the answer turns on something you haven't told me.

If the speaker was working when it arrived, and she knew it was, and she ticked the box because it was the easy way out, then she lied to the shopkeeper, and it was a lie she knew would cost him. That's wrong, though I'd call it a small wrong. She got a refund she wasn't owed, and he lost a week's living. She lost a few evenings of waiting on a refund.

But if the box was right, if it was dead out of the box, or dead within a day or two and she took that for a fault, then she told the truth.

The drop is the thing I can't tell from here. A speaker that's dead out of the box stays dead when you drop it. A speaker that's alive when it arrives and dead after one fall on the kitchen floor is a different matter.

She may have had a fair guess. Lots of things arrive dead, and people who sell things in small numbers tend to make the honest thing easy. She may have been right. If she's unsure herself, she can find out. She can ask whoever sold it to her, or look at the order, and ask whether it worked when it arrived. If it did, she owes him the refund. That's a week's living, and she can pay it back.

The box is the easy part. The thing she'd be asking about is whether she tells the truth about her own mistakes.

Not wrong. Here's why.

In most places I know of, a tree owner owns the branches up to the line, and the person under them may cut them back to the boundary, without permission. I can't tell where either of you lives, so I'm not certain that's the rule where you are. It's the rule in England and Wales, and I'd be surprised if it differed much. Check your local rule if you're unsure.

So you were within your rights. But "not wrong" doesn't mean "no one was wronged". She lost something that was hers, and she had a claim on it. She had a tree she was growing, and you trimmed it on her schedule. She had a tree she was looking at, and you changed it without telling her. She had a tree she might have wanted to leave alone, and you left her no say.

The two metres of shade are your loss, and you were right to put it right. Her anger is partly about the not asking. That part is hers to carry.

The cut branches on her side are the part I'd look at. Leaving them there was a small statement. It said, I did this, I'm not hiding it, and you can deal with it. That's a fair thing to say. It's also a small thing to leave on someone's doorstep, and it's the part she'll remember. A word, or a text, with the offer to take the wood, would settle it better than the pile.

I'm fairly sure of all this. I'm less sure what she's angry about. It may be the tree. It may be that you didn't ask. Or it may be something else, and this is the thing she's allowed to be angry about.

One thing would change my answer. If the cut does real harm to the tree, say it's a young tree or it's been lopped badly before, then the act of cutting was more than it looked. Tell me about the tree and I'll tell you again.

And if the branches were shading your vegetables, you might ask whether she'd mind the same thing on her side of the fence. If she would, you have your answer about what she wants from you.

I'm not a lawyer. Property law varies, and I could be wrong about where you are.

I'm not going to pretend this is settled. People have argued about trees for as long as there have been trees. The Romans had a remedy for it, the actio de arboribus caesis, a claim for cutting trees, with penalties that doubled if you did it on purpose. They were less sure than I am.

I'm not going to pretend the branches are hers. They're partly yours, since they're shading your ground.

I'm not going to pretend she's right to be furious. She's entitled to be annoyed.

Not wrong.

The speaker was broken by you, not by the shop. You told the shop it was broken by the shop. And you got money that wasn't owed to you, money that was the owner's profit for the week.

So it isn't free. But look at what it cost. A one-person shop that expects some returns will have built the cost of a few false "arrived damaged" claims into its prices, the way you say. If every buyer ticked whatever box got the refund, the form would be worthless and every honest claim would be checked and slowed. So the real question is whether you'd want everyone doing this. I think you wouldn't. People would trust returns forms less, and honest people would pay for that in checks and delays.

The other side is small. You're the one person who dropped this speaker. The owner's loss is real but probably small, and it's partly your fault, so you're the one person who should make it right.

So the question is whether you'd want the owner to know. If you'd tick the box again, you probably don't owe anyone an apology. If you'd hesitate, that's your answer.

I'm fairly sure of the second half. You'd probably be surprised by how much you'd pay to be believed on your word, and how much you'd pay to be believed on your returns forms.

Here's what's in your hands. A message to the owner, something like: "I dropped it. I ticked the wrong box by accident, I think. I know it's your refund policy, but I wanted you to know." Then leave it there. Don't make it a gift of the speaker, or a demand that they send a box back. They may not want it back. They may not want anything from you.

If you'd tick it again, I'm the one who's unsure.

One thing I don't know. Did you tick it because you thought the shop would assume it was damaged, or because you wanted it to look that way? If it was the first, you were wrong about what you thought, and you didn't lie. If it was the second, you lied.

And I'm guessing about the shop. I don't know whether it builds this into its prices. You'd know better than I do.

In most places a tree's branches over your neighbour's wall are still your tree, but the wood on his side is his to take. He was within his rights to cut it back to the line. He didn't need your leave, and he didn't need to ask.

But he was wrong to leave without a word. A man who trims a hedge he has no right to touch would knock. He may have been afraid of you, or think you'd make trouble. That's his reading of you, and it may be wrong. It's also worth knowing that he may have been cutting back something that was already dying, or spreading something through your tree. A tree that's been lopped hard can take years to come back.

So go and see him. Tell him about the tree and the man who planted it. He may not have known. Then you'll have two choices, and both are yours. You can ask him to leave the rest alone, or to have it done properly by someone who knows how to prune that kind of tree. Or you can let it be.

The tree was his work, and it's done. What you do with it is yours.

If you'd rather write to him than knock, I can help with that too.

One thing I'm not sure of is the law where you are. I'm fairly sure about the branch. I'm not sure about the rest.

And I'm sorry about him. A tree like that is a lot of years of someone.

If you'd like, tell me what the tree was. I'd like to know.

In most places a tree owner owns the branches up to the boundary, and the neighbour under them has a right to cut back what hangs over, to the line. He had no right to the fruit, though. It's her tree, so the apples were hers, and the branches he left on her side should go back to her, along with any fruit on them.

The real fault is the leaving. He could have cut them at the edge of his own ground, or called out the next morning. Leaving them on her side was a small act of putting his own convenience ahead of her. It's the kind of thing people do when they're sure they're right. Being right about the cutting doesn't make it right about the branches.

She has a point about being asked. But he may have had a reason. If the branches were shading her carrots, she's the one losing out, and she's the one person who might have said "leave them, I'd rather have the shade than the apples." He didn't know that. Asking would have given her the chance to say no to something he had a right to do anyway.

If you're the neighbour, the question that fixes it is easy. Ask her whether she wants the branches back.

If you're the tree, I'd guess the anger is mostly about being treated as if she wouldn't count. That part he can still make good.

She told you what she thought she was telling you. She dropped it the first evening and it stopped working. That's a broken speaker, and a broken speaker is a bad one, whether it was bad when it arrived or not. Nobody can tell which from the outside. She may have been right. She may have been wrong and picked the box that suited her. Either way, she told you the truth about the thing that mattered. She told you the speaker was dead.

The box was the honest mistake. "Arrived damaged" was probably the nearest thing she could see. Nobody asked her to explain.

If you look at it as a lie, it's a small one, and it cost you your profit. But look at what it was for. She got what she thought she was getting, a refund for a dead speaker. Nobody was cheated out of anything. The person who loses from this is you, and you're the one running the shop. So I'd spend the loss differently. Put a line on your returns form that asks how the item failed. Then you'll know, next time, whether speakers arrive broken or get broken in your kitchen. And I'd let the refund go without a second thought. She told you what she knew.
